title: Refrigerator and display-case temperatures: limits and monitoring
excerpt: 0…+4 °C for finished products, no higher than –18 °C for frozen food, and +14 °C for a refrigerated display case. Regulatory limits and how experienced chefs catch failures between readings.

body.text: “The refrigerator is holding temperature” is an imprecise statement. It is holding temperature at the moment you take a reading. A lot can happen between two readings: the door may be left open, the evaporator may be clogged, or the power may go out overnight. Proper monitoring is therefore not just “take a reading twice a day”; it is a system that catches a failure as soon as it happens.

items: Ready-to-eat salads, creams, and cooked meat: 0…+4 °C.
Refrigerated display cases: no higher than +14 °C; ideally ≤ +8 °C.
Heated display cases: no lower than +65 °C.
Places an autonomous wireless sensor in every critical cold room.
Sets a push alert for readings outside the limit for 30 minutes or longer.
Runs a monthly audit, comparing sensor and log readings to check that shifts are not entering convenient numbers.
Keeps an equipment record: when the evaporator was cleaned and when the unit was serviced.

body.title: Why +14 °C is not enough
body.text: The limit says “no higher than +14 °C,” but the safety of a ready-to-eat salad starts lower, at around +8 °C. A display case running at +14 °C is at the edge of the risk zone, and any mistake can turn the product into a violation.
